3. Out of the 6 witnesses examined in the case, let us discuss below the evidence of PW 6 who lodged the First Information Report and gave out the prosecution case. The witness stated that on 30-1-92 while carrying on investigation of Gulshan PS Case No. 9(1) 92 under sections 395/397 Penal Code he arrested accused SM Habibullah alias Hablu on 30-1-92. On being asked the said accused disclosed that one SMG is kept in the possession of one Talebur Rahman alias Taleb. The witness went to the residence of Taleb along with SM Habibullah and on his identification arrested Taleb. On query Taleb disclosed that one SMG was lying with one Abdul Matin whereupon the witness went to the house of Matin along with SM Habibullah and Taleb and arrested Matin who led the witnesses to the grocery shop at 71/1 Pirerbagh and brought out the SMG with magazine and 5 rounds of ammunition from inside the travel bag kept under the chowki in the shop. The accused appellant Matin could not give any satisfactory explanation and neither could show any valid document in respect of the said arms and ammunition. The arms and ammunition were seized and seizure list was prepared in presence of the witnesses who put there signature in the seizure list. On his lodging written ezaher First Information Report was recorded by the PW 4 ASI attached to Mirpur Police Station. The witness investigated the case and submitted charge sheet. The witness recorded the statements of the witnesses under section 161 CrPC and after investigation submitted charge sheet. In reply to cross- examination the witness stated that the name of the owner of the shop was not mentioned in the First Information Report and he also did not enquire about the owner of the shop. Rather, he presumed that the shop belonged to the accused-appellant Matin. It is stated that the grocery shop is at a distance of 5/6 kilometres from the DB office from where they went to Pirerbagh. The witnesses stated in cross- examination that he found 6/7 shops around the grocery shop at holding No. 71/1. He also admitted that he found the shop of A Majid Enterprise by the side of the grocery shop and he examined A Majid of the said Enterprise but he did not record his statement under section 161 CrPC. The witness admitted that he did not examine anybody from Nieman Electronic and the owners of other shops and they were also not cited as witnesses. He admitted that there are many other shops and rooms around the shop but he did not examine anyone amongst them. He also did not ask anything to the moazzen of the mosque. The witness also admitted that he did not examine the inmates of the two houses situated nearby the place of occurrence shop and he also did not mention their names. The witness denied the defence suggestion that the accused-appellant were implicated falsely and unnecessarily in the case and that the seizure list witnesses were not examined at the place and time of the recovery of the arms and ammunition. 

 6. We have taken up for discussion the evidence of the police witnesses first as their evidence relates to the alleged recovery of seizure of arms, lodging of First Information Report and submission of the charge sheet after holding investigation mainly for the reasons that the case was initiated at the instance of PW 6 who was the architect of the case. Let us now discuss the other witnesses who were members of the public to find out as to how far they have supported the prosecution case given out by the PWs. 4 5 and 6. 

 10. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the appellant Talebur Rahman alias Taleb in Criminal Appeal No. 720 of 1993. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate, appeared on behalf of the accused appellant Abdul Matin in Criminal Appeal No. 741 of 1993 and on behalf of the accused-appellant SM Habibullah Hablu alias Hablu in Criminal Appeal No. 869 of 1993. All the appeals having arisen out of the same judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed against the three accused-appellants placed for trial having been charged under section 19A and 19(t) of the Arms Act. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, the learned Advocate appearing along with Mr. ANM Gaziul Hoque, after placing the First Information Report, charge and the evidence on record and the judgment and order of the trial Court submitted that the conviction and sentence of the accused-appellants is based on surmises and conjectures rather than on legal evidence and the prosecution having failed to prove the case against the appellants beyond reasonable doubt the order of conviction and sentence cannot be sustained. It is submitted that PWs 5 and 6 who are stated to have gone to the place of occurrence in connection with investigation of a case under sections 395/397 Penal Code secured the arrest of three accused appellants one after another from different places and thereafter the SMG with some ammunition were alleged to have been recovered from inside the bag kept under the chouki of the shop under the name and style Roushan General Store but the police has miserably failed to prove the recovery of the arms by way of examining the owner and or any of the employees of the shop. It is submitted that on being asked the police admitted that there were so many shops and houses around the Roushan General Store but none of them was examined or even cited as witness in the case. Failure on the part of the police to find out the owner of the shop and to make him either an accused or cite him as a witness being fatal defect has cast serious doubt about the recovery of firearms and ammunition from the possession of the accused-appellants, the learned Advocate for the appellants submits. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan then submits that prosecution case as given out by PW 6 that arms and ammunition were recovered at the pointing of any of the accused-appellants in presence of the PWs 2 and 3 received a fatal blow when the said seizure list witnesses categorically denied to have seen the recovery of the arms and ammunition from the possession of the three accused-appellants whose presence at the place and time of recovery of the arms by the police was also not admitted by the witnesses. Mr. Khan submits that PWs 1, 2 and 3 who are the members of the public have totally demolished the prosecution case given out by the PWs 5 and 6, who are the police witnesses. It is also argued that the recovery of arms and ammunition and the seizure of the same by the police from the place which is not owned and possessed by the accused-appellant cannot make the appellants liable for keeping or possessing arms as defined under section 19A and 19(t) of the Arms Act. 

 12. Let us now see how far the prosecution has been able to prove the case against the accused under the Arms Act and, for that matter, under the Special Powers Act by adducing legal evidence. PWs 5 and 6, who are the investigating officers, have also deposed about the recovery and seizure of the arms and ammunition from the Grocery Shop at 71/1 Madhya Pirerbag, Mirpur. These two police personnels in their evidence sought to prove the case of recovery and seizure of the arms and ammunition in question. 

 13. Mr. MA Latif, the learned Advocate appearing for the State, submits that the judgment and order of conviction cannot be questioned on the ground that the conviction has been based only on the evidence of the police witnesses and the other witnesses are found to be unreliable. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the State cited the case of Nurul Islam vs. State reported in 8 BLD (1988) 106. 

 14. In the above quoted case similar points as to the reliability of the evidence of the witnesses of search and seizure of arms was raised and the learned Judge of the Single Bench while acquitting the accused from the charge under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act dealt with and elicited the provision of section 103 CrPC as follows: 

 "The object of the provision of section 103 CrPC is to ensure conducting of search in an impartial and fair manner and also to ensure that there is no 'planting' of incriminating articles by the police by any other person. There are quite a number of cases where the local witnesses of search and seizure by the police out of fear of the accused or their men or being gained over or for various other reasons depose falsely in favour of the accused to save the offender from legal punishment. Depending on the facts and circumstances of each case a Judge certainly may disbelieve a witness of search and seizures if it appears to him that he is deliberately making obliging statements in favour of the accused falsely in order to save him from legal punishment." 

 15. Though section 134 of the Evidence Act provides that no particular number of witnesses is required for the proof of any fact, but in order to convict an accused solely on the basis of solitary witnesses like the police officer or the person who made the search and seizure, the Judge must ensure that these witnesses are disinterested and the evidence is unimpeachable and unshaken and the other witnesses to the search who are alleged to have resiled from their previous stand, are unworthy of credit. 

 16. In the present case the evidences adduced by the police witnesses PWs 5 and 6 is not of unimpeachable character, rather it also suffers from inherent weakness being partisan in spirit. The police witnesses have not also been able to state as to whether the arms and ammunition were recovered from the exclusive possession and control of the appellants. PWs 1-3 cannot be disbelieved only because they did not harp with the tune with the police personnels. The prosecution has not also declared them hostile and cross examined them. The PWs 1-3 being independent witnesses their evidence is quite natural and probable having remained unrebutted. Furthermore, the prosecution has failed to examine the owner of the shop and or examine any witness of non-partisan character to bring home the charge against the appellants. Section 19 of the Arms Act under clause (f) provides that whoever has in his possession or under his control any arms, ammunition of military stores in contravention of section 14 or section 15 of the said Act shall be punished with imprisonment for life or any other rigorous imprisonment which shall not be less than seven years. The word "possession “means exclusive possession and the word "control" means effective control under this clause. Section19A only provides enhanced minimum punishment for offences under clauses (a) (c), (e) or (f) of section 19, if the offences are committed in respect of arms mentioned in the said section. Mere knowledge of the accused that the arms or ammunition were lying at the spot pointed out by him, in the absence of evidence or circumstances to show that he had himself kept the same there, or that he had exclusive possession over that spot or that none else had access to that spot, cannot bring the accused within the ambit of the offence under section(f) of section 19 of the Arms Act. This view of ours gets support from the case of Arshadullah and Nurul Islam vs. State reported in 21 DLR 684 wherein it is held: 

 "Mere knowledge of the accused that the arms or ammunition was lying at the spot pointed out by him, in the absence of evidence or circumstance to show that he had himself kept the same there or that he had exclusive possession over that spot or that none else had access to that spot, cannot make one liable for conviction under section 19 of the Act." 

 18. In the present case the accused appellants have had neither the possession and lorcontrol over the Roushan General Store, nor there is evidence that they ever visited this store and kept the arms and ammunition there. From the judgment of the trial Court also it appears to us that the order of conviction and sentence is based on the uncorroborated testimony of police witness only without taking into consideration that the evidence of such partisan witnesses is not unimpeachable being not independent and above board though the evidence of such partisan witnesses could not be found to be of unimpeachable character. 

 19. In view of the above we find that the assessment of evidence made by the trial Court is not at all satisfactory and that the guilt of the accused appellants have not been proved by reliable and satisfactory evidence and, therefore, we hold that the conclusion arrived at as to the guilt of the accused appellants by the learned trial Court is erroneous and hence cannot be sustained in law.
